chapter_theme: Paalai: the man's journey through the hot wasteland seen from home; the report of his going melts her eyes (13, 14), the road's killers and beasts make her fear for him (16, 23), omens of lizard and forehead promise his return (18, 19), and her heart follows him while the friend turns its swimming into his homecoming (21, 22). Five verses (14 to 17, 20) survive only in pieces.

13.reading: The friend tells the man that when she heard him speak of leaving by the long wasteland, where travellers hurry among stone-ringed cairns and run at the whistle of the Eyinar loosing their bows, her eyes, shaped like split tender mango, went soft with tears.
13.nuance: Nothing has happened yet except talk: the eyes give way at செலவுரைப்ப, the telling of the journey, so the poem shows the parting doing its harm before the man has moved. The first line is hard to construe (who hurries and harries the path), and the speaker is not named; the friend reporting to the man is the likeliest frame.

thinai_evidence.note: the eyes melt at the mere report of a journey through the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and pointed like a split tender mango

14.reading: Only fragments survive: fierce dogs give chase, something blossoms, and when the journey through the hot forest where the bushes have withered is spoken of, something will not stay; the end is lost.
14.nuance: போக்குரைப்ப repeats the situation of verse 13 (செலவுரைப்ப), so the poem probably turned on her response to the news of his going; நில்லா may have described her tears or her strength failing, but the lines that would say so are lost. The speaker is a guess from verse 13.

thinai_evidence.note: the report of a going through the hot forest

15.reading: Only the last lines survive: the one who went has crossed the hot forest of fierce sunrays, a place many dread (or: in a company of many), and a hill of crooked rocks is named before the text breaks off.
15.nuance: பல்லாருட்கண் can be divided as பல்லார் உட்கு (what many fear) or பல்லார் உள் கண் (among many), and the choice decides whether the line is about danger or company. The speaker is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched forest the man has crossed

16.reading: Of a damaged verse, what remains says that in the wasteland the fierce tiger brings down the charging elephant, and that 'our man' is somewhere in the lost close.
16.nuance: The tiger felling the elephant is the danger of the road at its most extreme: even the strongest beast is prey there, which is what makes the absent man's safety a question. Whether the lost close feared for him or promised his return cannot be told.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's road through a wasteland of killing beasts

17.reading: The stony wasteland where the wild gaur flee is named, with a young dark she-elephant and a tusker, and then the tears within kohl-lined eyes; the rest is lost.
17.nuance: A she-elephant and a tusker named together is where Sangam paalai often places a pair of creatures acting for each other, the textbook iraicchi; here the line breaks at மரு.... and no act survives, so the pair stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony wasteland and the eyes' tears

18.reading: The friend tells the woman that in the hard way among lovely hills, where wild cattle low and herds of beasts flee when the bow with its fine arrows twangs, the truthful-mouthed lizard has chirped as if it has seen the one who went through that graceless hot waste coming home.
18.nuance: வாய்மாண்ட praises the lizard's mouth as truthful, so the chirp is offered as testimony rather than hope; the verb கண்டு even gives the lizard eyes, as though it had seen the return before anyone at home. The hill with its lowing wild cattle is a kurinji scene set on the paalai road.

thinai_evidence.note: the man away on the hot waste and the omen of his return

19.reading: The friend tells the woman that the man who went for much wealth through the gravel forest, where the fierce proud tusker goes to stand asleep in the thin, broken shade of the lac-laden omai tree, will come back: the brightness climbing again onto her forehead says so.
19.nuance: The proof is in her own body: the pallor is receding before he arrives, and the friend reads the returning light (இவர்ந்து ஏறும், climbing up) as a sign, not as an effect of his coming. The tusker sleeping upright in shade too broken to cool it is how the forest's heat is shown; it does nothing a lover does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone through the gravel forest for wealth

20.reading: A damaged verse: something is made to fall, the one who went has crossed the ceaseless hot forest, and the surviving close says that our man will come.
20.nuance: வருவார் நமர் closes the verse with the promise verse 19 makes (வருவர்), so the speaker is probably the comforting friend, but the lost lines may have held the reason she gives.

thinai_evidence.note: the man crossing the hot forest, and the promise of his coming

21.reading: The woman tells her friend of young lifted breasts and moist teeth that, as the owl begins its short hooting and our man has crossed the forest where the rays burn and scorch, her heart goes after him, swimming the long way.
21.nuance: The dry forest is crossed by swimming: the heart moves through the scorched land as if through water, so the metaphor carries the effort and the danger of drowning into a waterless place. The owl's short cry marks the night falling as she speaks.

thinai_evidence.note: her heart following the man across the burning forest

comparisons.tenor: her heart crossing the long distance to him, as one swims a flood

22.reading: The friend asks the woman of bright jewels whether she really thinks the heart of the man who crossed the forest where robbers roam has parted from her, and says that he will cross back over the old mountain clefts and they will soon see him come.
22.nuance: Line 2 can also be read as a statement, 'you know he parted from you in mind (by his own resolve)', which would make the comfort harder; the question reading fits the confident close. The friend uses the same verb of swimming that the woman used of her heart in verse 21, now for the man's crossing home.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone through the robber-haunted forest

comparisons.tenor: the man crossing the mountain clefts on his way home

23.reading: The woman asks her friend whether the man who went in this very season, through the hot forest of rustling leaves where men with cruel arrows and twanging bows, their hearts empty of thought, run like Death with bows bent on killing, has come to no harm.
23.nuance: தொலைவிலர்கொல் turns on தொலைவு: as ruin it asks whether he is unharmed; as distance it asks whether he is not far away now, i.e. near home. The fear of the archers favours the first. சிந்தியா நெஞ்சு, hearts that do not think, makes the killers' danger their thoughtlessness rather than malice.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone this season through the killers' forest

comparisons.tenor: the archers who run with killing bows

24.reading: The woman tells her friend of chosen bangles that the road taken by the loveless one is, they say, the graceless, hard waste where, on the burning track as the mirage runs, the deer of the wilderness, craving, takes it in its mind for water and runs on without end.
24.nuance: The deer that runs forever after false water is close to the man who left for gain, but the poem draws no second correspondence and does not apply it, so it fails the two-pair condition of ullurai and stays scene; a reader may still hear it. பண்பில் (graceless) of the road and நண்பிலார் (loveless) of the man are set in one rhyme, so the land's want of kindness becomes his. The speaker could also be the friend, since ஆய்தொடி usually addresses the heroine.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard waste the loveless man took

links.note: Kural 1151: the friend (or the woman) tells the man that his promise of a quick return should be told to those still alive then. Kainnilai 13: told of his going by the long wasteland, her eyes went soft with tears.
links.teaches: Both answer the man's announcement of departure, but the Kural puts the threat to her life into argued words while the Kainnilai lets the friend report only the eyes giving way on hearing, so the pair shows the same reply could be made as a sharp argument or as a bare bodily fact laid before him.

links.note: Akananuru 387: on the road, a lizard's small click by the hero-stones makes even lords with elephants halt and turn back. Kainnilai 18: at home, the truthful lizard chirps as if it has seen the traveller's return.
links.teaches: Held together they show that the lizard's voice was trusted at both ends of the journey with opposite force, as a warning that turns travellers back on the road and as a promise of return to those at home, so the omen's sense depended on which way the hearer faced.

links.note: Akananuru 351: the returning man imagines the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him sounding at her ear as medicine for her aching shoulders. Kainnilai 18: the friend tells her the truthful lizard has chirped, seeing the traveller come.
links.teaches: The man in the Akananuru counts on the lizard to announce him and the friend in the Kainnilai reports that it has, so the pair gives both halves of one belief, that the traveller's approach reaches home through the lizard before he does.

links.note: Kural 1265: the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with her eyes. Kainnilai 19: the friend says the brightness returning to her forehead shows he is coming, before he has come.
links.teaches: On the Kural's reading the body recovers only from the sight of him and news cannot cure it, while the Kainnilai friend reads a recovery already begun as a sign of his return, so the two disagree on whether the body answers his presence or foreknows it.

links.note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes out looking for, since the beloved is already within it. Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart has gone after the man, swimming the long way through the scorched forest.
links.teaches: Both women speak of a heart that leaves to follow the man, but the Kural calls that going needless because he lives inside her, while the Kainnilai takes the heart's long swim as real, so the pair sets an inward answer to absence against the older picture of the heart travelling the road.

links.note: Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart swims the long way after him (நீந்து). Kainnilai 22: the friend says he will swim back over the old clefts (நீந்திப் பெயர்ந்தவர்) and they will soon see him.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the friend answers the woman's image with her own verb turned round, the heart swimming outward becoming the man swimming home, which shows how the friend's comfort in this book works by reversing the heroine's words rather than contradicting them.

links.note: Akananuru 29: the returned man tells his wife that only his body stayed in the burning waste for the work, while his foolish heart was with her. Kainnilai 22: the friend asks whether she thinks the heart of the man who crossed the robber forest has parted from her.
links.teaches: The friend's question in the Kainnilai presumes exactly what the man asserts on his return in the Akananuru, that the body went and the heart stayed, so the pair shows the body-heart split was a shared assurance used by the comforter before and by the man after the journey.

links.note: Natrinai 84: the woman reports that he will go (they say) by the hard waste where the mirage lures the deer, and excuses him as one who cannot live a home life unable to relieve beggars. Kainnilai 24: the woman reports that the hard waste where the deer runs after the mirage is, they say, the road of the loveless one.
links.teaches: The same reported road with the same mirage-chasing deer ends in opposite verdicts on the man, a duty that excuses him in the Natrinai and a want of love that condemns him in the Kainnilai, so the landscape fixed the scene while the poet chose the moral.

new_concepts.gloss: an omen read from the body or from creatures (sneezing, a throbbing eye, a lizard's chirp, an owl's cry) as a sign of the absent lover's thought or return
new_concepts.label_source: the Tholkappiyam's term for omens; the verses show the signs (பல்லி படும், நுதற்கு இவர்ந்து ஏறும் ஒளி)

source_issues: Verses 14, 15, 16, 17 and 20 have lost most of their lines (dotted gaps in the source); they are marked from what survives and flagged uncertain.
Verse 15: show flags that sangamtamil.com's text lacks lines 1 and 2, which are blank in ours too.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses and occasion words are null.

Verse 15 line 3 பல்லாருட்கண் divides two ways (பல்லார் உட்கு / பல்லார் உள் கண்); verse 18 line 2 ஏமாண் சிலையார்க்கும் is read as ஏ மாண் சிலை ஆர்க்கும் (the bow with fine arrows twangs), not as 'bowmen'; verse 23 line 4 தொலைவிலர் is ambiguous between unharmed and not far.
